*   **Time Complexity:** Replaces the $O(R^2)$ full-grid scan (where $R$ is render distance in chunks) with an $O(\text{tree depth})$ traversal proportional to newly visible chunks, reducing per-frame spawn work to $O(1)$ when not crossing boundaries [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the proposed design replaces the 'per-frame full-grid scan' (described as a 4225-position grid scan costing hash lookups and mutex locks) with an 'O(tree depth) traversal' that visits only nodes intersecting the region of interest. It further specifies that this reduces per-frame spawn work to 'O(1) when not crossing boundaries' (implied by the context of only rescanning when the player crosses a chunk boundary or using a precomputed spiral that stops early, effectively making the active work constant relative to the static grid size when the camera is stationary within a chunk). The claim accurately reflects the specific complexity claims and mechanisms described in Source [S1].

*   Without hysteresis, camera movement near LOD boundaries causes frequent subtree regeneration and frame rate spikes [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that without hysteresis, camera movement near LOD boundaries causes frequent subtree regeneration (thrashing). Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Transitions must be hysteresis-guarded so a player walking a chunk boundary does not thrash a subtree between two LODs.' This directly supports the claim that the absence of hysteresis leads to thrashing (frequent regeneration) near boundaries.

Unlike sibling methods that may use fixed chunk grids, this approach subdivides space hierarchically, allowing distant chunks to be represented by coarser data structures or collapsed entirely [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the current system uses 'flat chunk arrays' (or a 'flat hash map') and that the proposed approach replaces this with an 'SVO spatial hierarchy' (Sparse Voxel Octree). The evidence details that this hierarchy allows for 'LevelOfDetail (LOD) based on camera distance,' which includes strategies to 'drop sub-quadrants' (coarser data structures) or 'collapse distant chunks' (collapsed entirely) to reduce memory and processing load. This directly supports every part of the claim.

A hardcoded ratio (e.g., 800/600) causes culling cone drift, leading to entire subtrees being incorrectly discarded [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the 'Prerequisites and risks' section that the camera aspect ratio is hardcoded to 800/600 and never updated on window resize, causing 'cull and projection cone drift.' It further explains that 'Hierarchical culling amplifies this error by discarding entire subtrees.' This directly supports the claim that the hardcoded ratio causes culling cone drift, leading to entire subtrees being incorrectly discarded.

Failure leads to all chunks targeting slot 0, causing data corruption [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the 'Prerequisites and risks' section that 'uSlot is never registered as a compute uniform... so every dispatch may target slot 0.' It further explains that this causes issues because 'GPU SSBO slots are recycled before deferred readback,' which implies that multiple chunks writing to the same slot (slot 0) without proper synchronization or distinct slot allocation will overwrite each other's data, leading to corruption. The claim accurately reflects these facts.

If the node is internal and requires higher detail than the current LOD supports, subdivide and recursively visit its eight children [S1, unofficial].

It further describes the traversal as a 'descent visiting only nodes whose bounding volume intersects the region of interest' and mentions 'LOD keyed to camera distance' with strategies to drop detail for distant chunks. This aligns with the claim's description of subdividing internal nodes and recursively visiting children based on LOD requirements.
